title: Search autocomplete
summary: Precomputed prefix index with a strict latency budget.
prompt: Design search autocomplete: as a user types, show the top 10 suggested queries for the prefix, fast enough to feel instant.

requirements: Functional: return ranked completions for a prefix, reflecting popularity and recency, and suppress offensive suggestions.
Non-functional: a server latency of a few tens of ms at p99, very high read volume; suggestions may lag reality by minutes or hours.
Clarify: personalisation and languages (assume global popularity in one language).
estimation: 100M daily users × 10 searches × ~6 requests after debouncing ≈ 6B prefix requests a day ≈ 70,000/s average, a few times that at peak.
Keep the top ~100M distinct queries; with a precomputed top-10 list per prefix node, the serving index is tens of GB, so shard it or index only frequent prefixes.
api: Clients debounce (~100–150 ms), cancel in-flight requests and cache recent prefixes locally.
data: Query log events (query, time, locale) feed an aggregation job.
Serving structure: a trie whose nodes store a precomputed top-k list, or a prefix → top-k key-value map.
A blocklist applied when the index is built and re-checked when serving.
design: Read path: client → edge cache → suggest service → in-memory prefix index shard.
Write path: query logs → aggregation with time-decayed counts → periodic index builder → snapshot pushed to servers.
Servers load immutable snapshots and swap them atomically; the read path never writes.
deepDives: Precomputing top-k at each node makes a lookup O(prefix length), with no subtree walk at query time.
Ranking: exponentially decayed frequency lets trends rise and fade; personalisation can re-rank the top 50 using recent history.
Sharding by prefix range; very short prefixes are so hot they are served from cache or replicated everywhere.
bottlenecks: One- and two-character prefixes are the hottest keys: edge-cache them with short TTLs.
Rebuild time grows with vocabulary: build incrementally, or only index prefixes above a frequency threshold.
Breaking news needs faster freshness: merge a small real-time layer with the batch index.
tradeoffs: Top-k lists use much more memory than a plain trie in exchange for predictable latency.
Batch rebuilds are simple and safe but stale; a streaming layer adds freshness at a complexity cost.
Edge caching cuts load but slows the removal of a bad suggestion: keep TTLs short and support purges.

rubric.text: Set a latency budget and showed how the design meets it.
Used precomputed top-k per prefix, or justified an alternative.
Separated the offline build path from the online read path.
Ranked by popularity with recency decay.
Used client debouncing and caching to cut load.
Handled hot short prefixes and shard skew.
Added a freshness path for trending queries and weighed its cost.
